Margam
MAR-gum
n. (a Cistercian abbey in Glamorgan, founded 1147 as a daughter of Clairvaux; its nave serves as the parish church)
From the Welsh locality; a place name of uncertain derivation, recorded long before the abbey.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Margam was founded in 1147 in Glamorgan by Robert of Gloucester, a daughter of Clairvaux and one of the wealthiest Welsh houses, with granges along the coastal plain. Its twelve-sided chapter house, now roofless, is the finest in Wales, and its nave — like that at Holm Cultram — survives as the parish church, so that a Cistercian building has housed a Welsh congregation continuously for nearly nine centuries. The abbey also kept a chronicle that is a principal source for Welsh history. This dictionary has said repeatedly that the holiness was never in the stone, and that is true; it has also said that a lament over an empty church is permitted. Margam allows the third and happiest case: a building that is simply still in use. “Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ” (1Pe 2:5) is the real construction, and “that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD” (Psa 27:4) is a desire a plain parish church can serve as well as a cathedral.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines chapter house as the house where a chapter meets; nave as the middle or body of a church; and beauty as that assemblage of graces, or an assemblage of properties, which pleases the eye.

expand to see more

CHAPTER-HOUSE, n. A house or apartment where a chapter meets for the transaction of business.

NAVE, n. The middle or body of a church, extending from the balustrade of the choir to the chief entrance.

BEAUTY, n. An assemblage of graces, or an assemblage of properties in the form of a person or of any other object, which pleases the eye.

CONTINUANCE, n. A holding on or remaining in a particular state; perseverance; duration; a remaining in the same state.

GRANGE, n. A farm, with the buildings, stables, etc.; a farm house with the adjoining buildings.

Key Scripture

1Pe 2:5 — "Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ."

Psa 27:4 — "One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to enquire in his temple."

Psa 90:17 — "And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it."

Psa 26:8 — "LORD, I have loved the habitation of thy house, and the place where thine honour dwelleth."

Modern Corruption

A wealthy Glamorgan house of 1147 whose nave has served a Welsh congregation for nine centuries: the happiest of the fates in this dictionary, a building still in use.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the prayer of “And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it” (Psa 90:17) — a request for beauty to rest on people and for their work to be made to last, which is the right order of the two.

The live caution is wealth, which was Margam's condition and the usual Cistercian trajectory. A house with granges down a whole coastal plain had already travelled a long way from Cîteaux, and the honest note to end on is that its parish church survives because ordinary people needed it, not because its abbots were careful: “LORD, I have loved the habitation of thy house, and the place where thine honour dwelleth” (Psa 26:8).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew noam (H5278), beauty or pleasantness; Hebrew bayith (H1004), a house; Greek lithos (G3037), a stone; Greek oikos pneumatikos, a spiritual house; Hebrew kabod (H3519), glory or honour.

expand to see more

Hebrew noam (H5278) — pleasantness, beauty; “let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us” (Psa 90:17).

Hebrew bayith (H1004) — a house; the word of both temple and household.

Hebrew kabod (H3519) — weight, glory, honour; “the place where thine honour dwelleth” (Psa 26:8).

Greek lithos (G3037) — a stone; “as lively stones” (1Pe 2:5).

Greek pneumatikos (G4152) — spiritual; the kind of house and sacrifice Peter has in view.

Usage

"“One thing have I desired of the LORD” (Psa 27:4) — a desire a parish church can serve."

"“to offer up spiritual sacrifices” (1Pe 2:5) — the building that actually matters."

"“the work of our hands establish thou it” (Psa 90:17) — the only way anything lasts."
